slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by presenting this section as the point where constrained minimization becomes a certificate problem. The data of the program, the multipliers, and the active constraints all remain visible at once. Students should leave the first slide expecting every optimum to be explained by a balance equation, not by a blind search over feasible points.

slides.title: Ordinary Program Data
slides.notes: Emphasize that an ordinary convex program is more than an objective plus a feasible set. The separate functions f_i matter because multipliers attach to those functions. Two programs can describe the same feasible points but have different multiplier behavior if the constraint representation changes.

slides.title: Feasible Geometry
slides.notes: Use the picture to distinguish inactive constraints from active constraints. Inactive inequalities shape the feasible set globally but do not press on the optimum locally. Active constraints contribute normal directions, and equality constraints are always active because they must hold exactly.

slides.title: Kuhn-Tucker Coefficients
slides.notes: Introduce the weighted objective h_lambda as the algebraic device that trades constraints for prices. For feasible points, nonnegative weights on inequalities make h_lambda a lower certificate. A Kuhn-Tucker vector is special because the lower certificate reaches the primal optimum rather than merely sitting below it.

slides.title: Multiplier Existence
slides.notes: The relative interior condition is a constraint qualification. It rules out the kind of boundary-only feasible geometry where a separating hyperplane would have the wrong normalization. The slide should make existence feel like a separation theorem with enough room to separate the impossible strict system from the feasible one.

slides.title: KKT Conditions
slides.notes: Frame the KKT conditions as four tests that must be read together. Primal feasibility puts the point in the program, dual feasibility gives legal prices, complementary slackness deletes inactive inequality prices, and stationarity says the priced objective has no remaining first-order descent.

slides.title: Active Normal Balance
slides.notes: For differentiable data, stationarity becomes a vector balance. The negative objective gradient must lie in the cone generated by active inequality normals plus the span of equality normals. This is the geometric heart of the lecture: the optimum is where the feasible boundary can exactly push back.

slides.title: Lagrangian Saddle Point
slides.notes: Translate the conditions into a saddle statement. Holding x fixed lets the multipliers punish violations; holding lambda fixed turns the problem into minimizing the priced objective. At a saddle point, neither player can improve by moving alone, so the primal point and multiplier vector certify each other.

slides.title: Perturbation And Dual Value
slides.notes: Connect multipliers to sensitivity. The perturbation function records the best value after relaxing or tightening the constraint limits. A multiplier vector acts like a supporting price at the unperturbed problem, while the dual function g(lambda) gives lower bounds whose maximizers are exactly the Kuhn-Tucker vectors when they exist.

slides.title: Decomposition Principle
slides.notes: The decomposition principle is the computational payoff. If the objective and constraints split into blocks except for a small coupling equation, a multiplier vector turns one coupled problem into independent priced subproblems. The global work moves to finding the shared price vector.

slides.title: Quadratic KKT Lab
slides.notes: Use the small quadratic example as a numerical anchor for the notebook invariant. The unconstrained point lies beyond the halfspace, so the optimizer is its projection onto the active line. The multiplier equals the amount of normal correction, and both stationarity and complementary slackness reduce to visible zero residuals.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the certificate flow. The section begins with program data, asks when legal prices exist, proves that KKT conditions are equivalent to a Lagrangian saddle point, and then uses the same multipliers for dual value recovery and decomposition. The practical habit is to inspect feasibility, activity, prices, and residuals together.
